title: Cultivation Hazards: Tools, Machinery, Electrical and Work Areas

content.overview: Cultivation work combines agricultural tools, powered equipment, wet floors, electricity, lifting and repetitive tasks. Safety starts by identifying the hazard, controlling it at the source where possible, using safe procedures and PPE, and keeping work areas maintained.

vocabulary.definition: A condition or activity with potential to cause injury, illness or damage.
A physical change that reduces exposure to a hazard without relying only on worker behavior.
Personal protective equipment worn to reduce exposure when other controls do not fully remove the hazard.

sections.title: Tools require condition and technique
sections.body: Cutting tools, ladders and powered equipment can cause serious injuries when damaged, unguarded or used incorrectly. Inspection, maintenance and manufacturer instructions are basic controls.

sections.title: Wet cultivation spaces increase slip and electrical risk
sections.body: Irrigation leaks, cords and equipment can create overlapping hazards. Clear walkways, appropriate electrical protection and prompt cleanup reduce preventable incidents.

sections.title: Control hierarchy is stronger than PPE alone
sections.body: Removing a hazard, separating workers from it or redesigning the task is generally stronger than relying solely on protective equipment or attention.

workedExamples: A damaged extension cord near irrigation water should be removed from service rather than covered with tape and left in use.
A repeated trip hazard from hoses is better addressed by routing and securing them than by telling workers to step carefully.
commonMistakes: Treating PPE as the only safety control.
Leaving wet floors or blocked aisles for later cleanup.
content.practicalApplication: Walk the workspace looking for cutting, electrical, trip, lifting and machinery hazards. Document the hazard, control, responsible person and correction status rather than relying on memory.
content.summary: Safe cultivation work is designed, not improvised. Equipment condition, layout and source controls should reduce hazards before PPE becomes the final layer.
